title: Galaxies in a swarm of star clusters
caption: The giant elliptical galaxy NGC 4874 in the Coma Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4874 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 350 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The brightest object here, on the right, is NGC 4874, a star-like core wrapped in a hazy halo. Other cluster galaxies float around it like flying saucers. The space around it is peppered with points of light, almost all of them globular clusters, each holding many hundreds of thousands of stars.

Sitting at the heart of the Coma Galaxy Cluster, NGC 4874 is a giant elliptical galaxy roughly ten times the size of the Milky Way. Its strong gravity holds onto more than 30 000 globular clusters, more than any other galaxy we know of.

A few of those points turned out to be ultra-compact dwarf galaxies, only about 200 light-years across and mostly made of old stars. Astronomers think they are the leftover cores of small elliptical galaxies that were stripped of their gas and outer stars in violent encounters within the cluster.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.23 x 3.35 arcminutes) and distance (350 million light years), the frame spans roughly 329,000 × 341,000 light-years. Its light set out about 350 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, combining visible and near-infrared exposures. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The near-infrared part is invisible to the eye, and the thousands of faint star clusters need Hubble's sharp, long exposures to be seen.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Small smudges in the background are galaxies far beyond the cluster, whose light spent anywhere from several hundred million to billions of years traveling to us. The Coma galaxies themselves are about 350 million light-years away.
A faint blue satellite trail crosses the whole frame from upper left to lower right, a rare sight because Hubble sees only a tiny patch of sky at once.
alt: A bright galaxy with a hazy halo on the right, surrounded by many point-like star clusters, other galaxies, and a faint blue line crossing the frame.
